## What is TableVault?

TableVault is a centralized data repository (backed by ArangoDB) that stores
**item lists** — ordered collections of data items. Every item list has a
unique name and belongs to one of four types:

| Type          | Stores                                         |
|---------------|------------------------------------------------|
| **file**      | References (paths) to external files           |
| **document**  | Text strings (paragraphs, logs, notes, etc.)   |
| **embedding** | Fixed-dimension float vectors                  |
| **record**    | Structured rows (dict with predefined columns) |

------------------------------------------------------------

## How data gets into TableVault

Among the stored evaluations, the highest accuracy is obtained by mean pooling over non-special tokens (0.703), followed by CLS pooling (0.686), while max pooling and last-4-layer mean pooling both reach 0.684 and standard mean pooling over all final-layer tokens is lowest at 0.650. However, the class-wise reports reveal that max pooling and last-4 mean pooling completely fail to recover the non-paraphrase class (non-paraphrase recall = 0.00, paraphrase recall = 1.00), and CLS pooling is only marginally better (non-paraphrase recall = 0.01). This pattern is consistent with near-majority-class prediction on MRPC, whose stored support counts are 279 paraphrases versus 129 non-paraphrases. In contrast, standard mean pooling is the only strategy that meaningfully separates both classes, with non-paraphrase recall 0.74 and paraphrase recall 0.61, though its headline accuracy is lower. Thus, if accuracy alone is used, excluding special tokens appears best; if balanced discrimination matters, mean pooling over tokens is more informative. The evidence also suggests that averaging the last 4 layers does not improve over max pooling in these stored runs. A limitation is that the repository records are workflow summaries rather than a perfectly controlled ablation, and some item names indicate minor procedural differences beyond pooling itself (for example, median-threshold scoring or excluding special tokens), so conclusions should be interpreted as comparative evidence from the stored experiments rather than a definitive causal benchmark."}
